source.title: Large Language Models Relearn Removed Concepts
source.authors: M. Lo; Shay B. Cohen; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: The study uses neuron-level concept identification, pruning, and activation analysis to study relearning. It does not audit the share of neurons with one main job or test any of the listed explanation claims; its polysemanticity results follow deliberate pruning and retraining.
record.gate_note: The study deliberately prunes the most salient 50% of neurons for a concept and retrains the models. Its resulting saliency redistribution and polysemanticity observations concern induced relearning, not the prevalence of single-job neurons in unmodified models. It does not evaluate explanations on held-out activations or score explanations by simulated activations. NER performance recovery tables are not included as rows because they measure task performance, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study prunes the top 50% of location-concept neurons in NER-fine-tuned DistilBERT, DistilGPT2 and GPT-2, retrains, and tracks per-layer concept saliency and highest-activating-token similarity. It uses probeless concept-neuron ranking as a tool. It never estimates how many neurons have one main job (V1, V2). It has no InceptionV1 or pose analysis (V3), no tool or architecture comparison of interpretable share (V4), and no attribution graphs (V5). It does not test explanations on held-out activations (V6) or score them by simulated activations (V7). Its 'polysemantic' observation is induced by deliberate pruning and retraining, so it says nothing about the prevalence of multi-job neurons in unmodified models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress two further points. Pruned concepts initially in later layers are remapped to earlier or middle-layer neurons. Those neurons were 'primed' because they previously captured similar concepts. The authors caution that the saliency–similarity link is tentative.
record.recipe_differences: This is a pruning-and-retraining study of concept relocation and recovery, not a neuron-job audit or evaluation of explanations against held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed redistribution differs by model: DistilBERT and DistilGPT2 show increased saliency in middle layers, while GPT-2 is described as redistributing saliency more evenly. The study also reports different outcomes for concept-targeted versus random pruning.

fits_no_version.finding: After targeted pruning of location-concept neurons and retraining, per-layer concept saliency shifts: layer 4 rises in DistilBERT, layers 4–5 in DistilGPT2, and GPT-2 evens out (Tables 5–7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept saliency relocates across layers after targeted neuron pruning and retraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Retrained neurons activate on both the pruned concept and their prior top tokens. Examples are DistilBERT neuron 4148 (Table 8) and neuron 2405 (Table 21). Most DistilGPT2 similarity scores exceed 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning and retraining induces neurons to blend old and new concepts; this is induced polysemanticity, not its natural prevalence.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: The study examines only DistilBERT, DistilGPT2, and GPT-2, and its concept-remapping results follow deliberate pruning and retraining. It notes that the precise relationship between saliency and similarity is unclear and reports relatively large standard deviations for those measures (0.205 and 0.199).
record.rows_left_out: Table 4's random-pruning saliency values are omitted because the flattened values do not permit reliable assignment to layers. NER performance tables are omitted because they report task-performance recovery rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No pole or neuron job-share audit; no Qwen3-32B.
No single-job share estimates in any model or scale; the models are used only for pruning and relearning.
No vision models, no InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, no pose or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of interpretable-neuron share across tools, regularization or architectures.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
Highest-activating tokens are inspected, but explanations are never tested for predicting activations elsewhere.

record.verdict_notes: No version is tested, so there are no verdicts. 'uses_without_test' or 'assumes' with T4 is reasonable, since the study relies on concept neurons existing and being identifiable via probeless ranking. Table 14 in the appendix appears to duplicate Table 11's recall and F1 values, which suggests a copy error, but it is not used in any row. Row states marked 'observed' carry no meaning for the claim, because all rows link to 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: No estimate of the Qwen3-32B pole shares or of single-job, two-job, or not-understood neuron proportions.
The study examines DistilBERT, DistilGPT2, and GPT-2 for induced concept relearning, not the claimed shares across models, architectures, or scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose feature, or recursive-generalization test.
No comparison of interpretability estimates across tools or architectures, and no InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
The study does not test explanations against where a neuron fires beyond the examples used to write them.
The study does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: It uses concept-neuron ranking as a tool and does not test any version of the claim.

tranche.reason: It uses probeless concept-neuron ranking and pruning as tools to study relearning. It never estimates what share of neurons have one main job, and the polysemanticity it reports is induced by pruning. T6 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: Both rows match the text. The cited statement puts person-names neuron 2405 (Table 21) under the location-names result. The polysemanticity reported comes from pruning plus retraining (the authors say 'neuroplasticity-induced'), so it is no measure of natural neuron cleanliness.

statements.correction: Location names: DistilBERT neuron 4148 (layer 5) activates on new location tokens (Maltese, Malaysian) and on base-model tokens (Bronze, Egyptian) after 8 retraining epochs (Table 8). Person names: DistilBERT neuron 2405 keeps 'exist' and gains person-name tokens (Table 21, App. C.2). DistilGPT2, location names, 8 epochs: most concept similarity scores > 0.5 (§6.4, Fig. 7).
statements.problem: Neuron 2405 is cited as a location-names example, but in the text it comes from the person-names pruning experiment (Table 21, Appendix C.2, DistilBERT). The 4148 and DistilGPT2 >0.5 parts are right. Calling it 'induced' matches the authors' own phrase 'neuroplasticity-induced polysemanticity'.
